To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
emphasizing subgroup identity prior to superordinate negotiation can have both positive and negative consequences for the negotiation process.
social identity is an important determinant of negotiation processes, and that the way in which social identities are represented can influence the success of negotiations.
emphasizing subgroup boundaries prior to negotiation increases identification at the subgroup level but also increases satisfaction with the negotiation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of social identity in the resolution of social conflict.
how the process of negotiation is shaped by the social identities of participants, and how this process can influence the outcomes of negotiation.
the relationship between social identity and negotiation and the role of social identity in conflict resolution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the social identity approach to intergroup relations is not a simple matter of ingroup bias.
social identity is important to the negotiation process, but the nature of the social identity that is important varies with the context.
social identity and negotiation processes are not mutually exclusive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
when people are able to identify at both the superordinate and subgroup levels they are more satisfied with the outcome of the negotiation process.
social identity and negotiation are not incompatible, but rather that they can be complementary.

The main takeaway from our work is that
social identity can be a powerful force in negotiation, but it is important for negotiators to recognize when it may be a hindrance and when it may be helpful.
social identity is a key component of conflict, and that it is not only important to understand how it shapes conflict, but also how it can be harnessed to help resolve it.
identity-based group conflict is not always detrimental to negotiation.
